Raman modes at high frequencies (P4-P7) are related to the vibrational modes of the [P2Se6] 4clusters, while the low-frequency peaks (P1-P3) are attributed to the vibrations involving the heavy Mn atoms [34]. As for the P1 peak, it appears at 82.8 cm  1 , which is related to magnetic Mn ions. A previous study found that a phonon peak ~ 86 cm  1 appeared below TN and disappeared above TN [34]. For our experimental result, P1 can still be observed at room temperature (Enlarged P1 region in Fig. S5), which will be discussed later. Interestingly, it was found that the intensity of P1 is enhanced at low temperatures. We normalized and plotted the intensity as a function of temperature (Fig. 2e). The intensity of P1 fi rstly exhibits a sharp drop and then remains stable as the temperature increases from 25 K to 300 K. Two-magnon scattering and Fano resonance of NiPS3 . In order to study the thickness dependence of the antiferromagnetic ordering, we measured the temperature dependence of the Raman spectra as a function of the number of layers down to the monolayer limit. Figure 3a shows the temperature dependence of the Raman spectrum of bulk NiPS3 measured in the crosspolarization con fi guration. Suppression of several phonon peaks makes it easier to monitor the two-magnon signals in the crosspolarization con fi guration. In these data, we observe that the twomagnon signals gradually grow and shift towards higher frequencies as the temperature decreases below T N. These observations are typical of antiferromagnetic materials, where the twomagnon signals redshift and become broader and weaker as the spectral weight is shifted to QES when the temperature is increased 27,28,33,34 . We have carried out similar measurements for few-layer samples with different thicknesses (see Supplementary Fig. 6) and the results are summarized in Fig. 3c -f. The peak position, intensity, and width of the two-magnon signals show little dependence on the number of layers from bulk all the way down to two layers. The coupling strength of Fano resonance, represented by |1/ q |, also shows dramatic enhancement below bulk T N. On the other hand, the spectrum of monolayer NiPS3 seems to have a qualitatively different temperature dependence from that of samples with other thicknesses. For example, Fig. 3b shows the temperature dependence of the Raman spectrum of monolayer NiPS3 as a function of temperature. Unlike other samples thicker than monolayer, the two-magnon feature is not well de fi ned even when the temperature is much lower than the bulk T N. The position of the two-magnon peak is also considerably lower in frequency than in the case of thicker samples. Furthermore, the peak P9 does not show any indication of Fano resonance.

Thus, P3 becomes weaker and is coupled with phonon mode (P2) when the temperature increases. It features with an apparently broad peak at 35 K and 45 K, indicating the strong phonon-magnon coupling. So we consider decoupled P3 mode as a one-magnon mode and the whole mode at 110-120 cm  1 as a coupled phonon-magnon mode. To investigate how thermal fl uctuations affect one-magnon excitation, we plot the low-frequency Raman spectra of exfoliated MnPSe3 with different thicknesses (Fig. 5e), which are obtained at 25 K. Despite the weak Raman signals, the abnormal Raman peaks (P3) caused by one-magnon can still be observed ranging from bulk to 3.98 nm (~5L). The Raman evidence of one-magnon in 2D MnPSe3 not only supports the existence of magnetism, but also motivates further research in magnonics and magnon-based spintronics.

In this work, we present a spectroscopic study of few-layer to bulk MnPS3 from cryogenic temperature to room temperature. We propose a formula to quickly and accurately identify the layer numbers of MnPS3 based on optical contrast spectra. All Raman modes are also identi fi ed by polarized Raman measurements. More interesting, we found three magnetic transition temperatures at around 120, 80, and 55 K based on temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy.

The samples were prepared from bulk MnPS3 crystals (about 1 mm) onto Si substrates covered with a SiO2 fi lm of 90 nm using the micromechanical exfoliation technique. Raman measurements and optical contrast measurements were undertaken in backscattering geometry with a JobinYvon HR800 system equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled charge-coupled detector (CCD). The Raman spectra were collected with a 100 × objective lens (NA = 0.9) and a 1800 lines/mm grating at room temperature, while a 50 × longworking-distance objective lens (NA = 0.5) was used for lowtemperature measurements. The excitation wavelength was 488 nm from an Ar + laser. The typical laser power was about 0.17 mW to avoid laser heating on the sample. A tungsten halogen lamp was used as a light source for optical contrast measurements.
